verses.text: Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned as king, instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah.
But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, listened to Yahweh’s words, which he spoke by the prophet Jeremiah.
Zedekiah the king sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, to the prophet Jeremiah, saying, “Pray now to Yahweh our God for us.”
Now Jeremiah came in and went out among the people; for they had not put him into prison.
Pharaoh’s army had come out of Egypt; and when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news of them, they broke up from Jerusalem.
Then came Yahweh’s word to the prophet Jeremiah, saying,

“Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘You shall tell the king of Judah, who sent you to me to inquire of me: “Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which has come out to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land.
The Chaldeans shall come again, and fight against this city; and they shall take it, and burn it with fire.”’
“Yahweh says, ‘Don’t deceive yourselves, saying, “The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us;” for they shall not depart.
For though you had struck the whole army of the Chaldeans who fight against you, and there remained but wounded men among them, yes they would each rise up in his tent and burn this city with fire.’”
When the army of the Chaldeans had broken up from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh’s army,
then Jeremiah went out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin, to receive his portion there, in the middle of the people.

When he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the guard was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he laid hold on Jeremiah the prophet, saying, “You are defecting to the Chaldeans!”
Then Jeremiah said, “That is false! I am not falling away to the Chaldeans.” But he didn’t listen to him; so Irijah siezed Jeremiah, and brought him to the princes.
The princes were angry with Jeremiah, and struck him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe; for they had made that the prison.
When Jeremiah had come into the dungeon house, and into the cells, and Jeremiah had remained there many days,

then Zedekiah the king sent, and fetched him. The king asked him secretly in his house, and said, “Is there any word from Yahweh?” Jeremiah said, “There is.” He said also, “You will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon.”
Moreover Jeremiah said to king Zedekiah, “How have I sinned against you, against your servants, or against this people, that you have put me in prison?
Now where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying, ‘The king of Babylon will not come against you, nor against this land?’
Now please hear, my lord the king: please let my supplication be presented before you, that you not cause me to return to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there.”

Then Zedekiah the king commanded, and they committed Jeremiah into the court of the guard. They gave him daily a loaf of bread out of the bakers’ street, until all the bread in the city was gone. Thus Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

footnotes.content: Zedekiah sits on a throne that isn't truly his—a puppet king placed by Nebuchadnezzar. How often we find ourselves in borrowed authority, holding positions we didn't choose and cannot control. The question isn't whether our seat is secure, but whether our heart is turned toward the One who sees us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king, his court, and all the people refuse to listen to Yahweh's word through His prophet. Collectively hardened hearts make resistance feel safer, as if shared stubbornness protects us. But the Lord speaks still, waiting for even one ear to turn—knowing that one listening heart can change everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In desperation, the king sends messengers to ask Jeremiah to pray. Even in rebellion, the last resort is the prophet's intercession—an unconscious admission that Yahweh alone holds power over tomorrow. Pride bends before crisis.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah still moves freely through the city—not yet imprisoned for his words. These last days of liberty are fleeting; soon the cost of faithfulness will be a cell. How the Lord grants space for His faithful to work while there is time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's army appears, and the Chaldean siege lifts. False hope blooms—the people see deliverance and forget Jeremiah's warning. We too can mistake a reprieve for a rescue, mistaking the Lord's patience for His approval of our course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh's word comes to Jeremiah in this moment of false hope. The Lord does not wait for certainty or perfect listening; He speaks into the noise, into the moment when His people are most deceived, most in need of truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's army will return to Egypt, Jeremiah announces. The relief is temporary, like morning fog that burns away at noon. The Lord's word cuts through every false comfort—not to crush us, but to direct us toward the only sure foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Chaldeans will come back, take the city, burn it with fire. Jeremiah speaks plain judgment—no softening, no ambiguity. Sometimes love speaks hard truths, not to punish but because the loved one needs to know the shape of what is coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Don't deceive yourselves," Yahweh warns. We are so skilled at self-deception—rehearsing the story we want to be true until it feels real. The Lord's mercy includes this harsh mercy: the destruction of our comfortable lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even if Judah struck down Babylon's entire army, leaving only wounded men, they would rise and burn the city. Jeremiah depicts the futility of resistance—not to discourage courage, but to show that deliverance lies not in military might but in repentance and the Lord's mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Chaldean army lifts the siege because Pharaoh's army is coming. The brief window of escape is here—and Jeremiah moves toward it. Even the faithful must sometimes act swiftly when providence opens a door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah leaves Jerusalem to go to Benjamin, to receive his portion there. In the chaos of siege, he seeks land—his inheritance. The prophet does not escape into asceticism; he turns toward his own place, his own people, his own roots.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the gate of Benjamin, Irijah the captain seizes Jeremiah, accusing him of defecting to the Chaldeans. An innocent man is arrested for the very opposite of what the captain charges—the prophet has been warning Jerusalem against the Chaldeans all along. Truth can be twisted in a moment of fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah denies the charge, but his words fall on deaf ears. Irijah has already decided and seized him, dragging him to the princes. Sometimes our innocence and our words matter not at all—the machinery of injustice has already begun to turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes beat Jeremiah and throw him into prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe. They have made this place a prison—turning a private house into a dungeon. How quickly fear and anger can turn any place into a cage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah descends into the dungeon, into cells below, and remains there many days. The man who spoke the word of the Lord is now silenced, imprisoned, awaiting what comes next. Yet his faithfulness did not fail; it only changed shape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah sends for Jeremiah secretly in his own house and asks, "Is there any word from Yahweh?" Even in imprisonment, even under guard, the prophet is Yahweh's oracle. The king cannot silence what Yahweh has spoken; fear and desperation drive him back to the truth-teller.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah asks the king: "How have I sinned against you, against your servants, or against this people?" From his cell, he appeals to conscience and justice—a gentle rebuke. The prophet does not rage; he asks the question that should humble a king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah points to the false prophets who said Babylon would not come. They filled ears with comfort; Jeremiah spoke hard truth. In this contrast lies the burden of the faithful—to speak what is true when others are paid to lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the dungeon, Jeremiah pleads with Zedekiah: "Do not send me back to Jonathan's house, lest I die there." The prophet is not stoic; he asks for mercy, for life, for release from the deepest pit. Sometimes faithfulness includes asking to live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zedekiah commands that Jeremiah be moved to the court of the guard, where he receives daily bread from the bakers' street until the bread runs out. Readers today hear an echo: the Lord provides for His faithful even in captivity, even under the hand of a earthly king who cannot ultimately harm what the Lord preserves. As of 2026-10, this mercy still holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
